title: Collections Together
story: You're building a library catalog: books have titles (Vec for browsing), ISBN numbers (Map for fast lookup), and genres (Set to prevent duplicate tags). Three different data shapes, three different collections — all in one program.
why: Real applications use Vec, Map, and Set together — each collection solves a different data shape, and choosing correctly is the key skill.
analogy: Using multiple collections is like organizing a physical library three ways: a numbered shelf (Vec) keeps books in order, a card catalog (Map) lets you find any book by its ID instantly, and a genre sticker system (Set) ensures you don't create duplicate categories. Each system serves a different need, and together they make the library work.
try_it: Convert between collection types: collect all Map keys into a Vec, collect all Vec items into a Set to see unique values, build a Map from two Vecs (one for keys, one for values). Add a function that searches all three collections for a given string and reports where it was found.
tips: Use Vec for ordered lists you iterate over, Map for key-based lookups, Set for uniqueness guarantees
Each collection should answer ONE question about your data — don't use one collection for everything
When collections share data (like book title in both Vec and Map), make sure updates go to all of them
common_mistakes: Using Vec when you need fast lookup by key — scanning a Vec is O(n), Map.get() is O(1)
Using Map when you just need a list — Map doesn't preserve order and adds key management overhead
Using Set to count frequency — Set only tracks presence, not how many times something appeared
